newsitem.title: DUBAI: Velayati says Iran, Saudi want to build trust.
newsitem.headline: Velayati says Iran, Saudi want to build trust.

text.p: Iran's Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati said on Sunday Iran and Saudi Arabia had agreed on the need to build trust between the two major oil states.

Velayati, who planned further talks later on Sunday, reiterated at a news conference in Riyadh Iran's opposition to U.S. and other Western forces staying in the oil-rich region, saying security was the responsibilty of regional states.
The Iranian foreign minister was on his first visit to Saudi Arabia since 1993 after years of often tense relations between two of the world's biggest oil exporters.

"The two sides agreed that the basis for consolidating mutual relations is to strengthen mutual trust and expand cooperation," Velayati said after talks with Saudi King Fahd and Foreign Minister Prince Saud al-Faisal.
He said strong ties were a "joint demand" by the countries. Saudi newspapers said on Sunday Velayati proposed setting up of cooperation committee to work to overcome mistrust.

Relations between radical Shi'ite Iran and Sunni-ruled Saudi Arabia are uneasy and they are bracing for more tension during the annual haj pilgrimage to the holy cities of Mecca and Medina in mid-April.
Iran insists its pilgrims hold political rallies to denounce Israel and the United Staes. Saudi insists the haj should not be politicised.
Riyadh and Tehran are also at odds over U.S. and other Western forces in the Gulf. Iran says the troops, including about 5,000 U.S. forces in Saudi Arabia, increase regional tension.

U.S. media reports have linked Iran to the June bombing of a U.S. military housing complex in eastern Saudi Arabia that killed 19 U.S. servicemen. Iran denied any involvement and Saudi officials said the probe was not finished.
The Iranian minister, who started a tour of 10 countries on Sunday that includes Syria, Turkey, Sudan, Uganda and the Czech republic, is to visit other Gulf Arab states.
Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani is inviting heads of Moslem states and governments to a summit of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC), the world's largest Moslem body.

"I have extended the invitation to the king and delivered a message from the Iranian president," Velayati said. "King Fahd welcomed the invitation and said he would participate as much as it would be possible for him."
Diplomats said Saudi Arabia's presence at the summit would be crucial. The kingdom is home to Islam's two holiest shrines and its commercial capital Jeddah is the OIC base.

Gulf-based diplomats and analysts doubted King Fahd would go to Tehran, but said Crown Prince Abdullah would be expected to attend the Moslem world's most important gathering. Velayati was to meet Prince Abdullah on Sunday after a visit to the holy city of Medina.
Iranian media have called Velayati's visit highly significant and said it was likely to ease tension. Gulf Arabs have accused Tehran of interfering in their internal affairs.
